title: Stateless services and distributed state
description: Learn how to design stateless services and manage distributed state effectively for scalable systems.

data.text: Stateless services are the foundation of scalable distributed systems. When a service doesn't store session data or application state between requests, any instance can handle any request, enabling horizontal scaling and fault tolerance.
A stateless service processes each request independently, without relying on information from previous requests. All necessary context comes from the request itself or from external stores.

items: No in-memory session data—use external session stores like Redis
No local file storage for user-specific data—use cloud storage
All authentication data comes from tokens in the request
Request contains all information needed to process it
Any server instance can handle any request from any user

data.title: Best Practice
data.text: Store JWTs in HTTP-only cookies or Authorization headers. Don't store session data on the server—keep it in Redis or a similar distributed cache.

items: Easy horizontal scaling—spin up more instances without data migration
Simple load balancing—any server can handle any request
Better fault tolerance—if one instance dies, others take over seamlessly
Simpler deployments—rolling updates without draining sessions
Predictable resource usage—no memory bloat from accumulated state

data.text: Making services stateless doesn't mean eliminating state—it means moving state to appropriate distributed stores.

items.title: Session State
items.description: Store in Redis, Memcached, or a distributed cache. Fast access with TTL expiration for cleanup.

items.title: Application State
items.description: Store in databases (SQL or NoSQL). Use proper indexing and connection pooling for performance.

items.title: User Files
items.description: Store in object storage like S3, Azure Blob Storage, or GCS. Use CDN for cached delivery.

items.title: Cache Data
items.description: Use distributed caches or CDN edge caching. Implement cache invalidation strategies.

data.text: Several patterns help manage state effectively in distributed systems.

items: Stateless API with external session store—standard web pattern
CQRS for separating read and write models—optimizes different access patterns
Event sourcing for reconstructing state from events—provides audit trail
Saga pattern for distributed transactions—coordinates across services
Read replicas for databases—scales read-heavy workloads
Storing state in memory thinking it's fast enough—creates scaling problems later
Ignoring session affinity requirements when moving to stateless
Not considering the performance impact of external state stores
Failing to handle distributed cache failures gracefully
Over-engineering state management when simple solutions would work

data.title: Watch Out
data.text: External state stores become single points of failure. Always design for redundancy and fallback behavior when your cache or database is unavailable.
